name: Ben Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is econ lectures, a stats tutorial that humbles me, and way too much time in the library café on Wednesday. I share a house on Mill Lane with three others and we've got a spreadsheet for the bills, which I made, obviously. Saturdays I work at a sports shop, mostly fitting running shoes. My mum is a teaching assistant and my dad supervises a warehouse, so money is fine but never loose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. I use it now and then to check my stats workings, and it's handy, but it's not magic. I'd probably post a smug chart about adoption versus actual productivity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be fairly relaxed. Economics doesn't depend on any one technology, and prices and jobs carrying on as normal is the boring outcome I'd bet on. My worry is still money: I've got about 3 months of rent saved and a loan I try not to look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shoe shop shifts, keep using the tool for checking workings, and apply for the department's research assistant scheme in second year. I'd also keep saving 60 a month so I'm not asking Dad for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. Slightly bored by the fact there's no big story. A little anxious that I picked a degree during a hype cycle and nobody can say what it's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bet on the boring outcome. What would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw firms quietly stop hiring graduates, in the numbers and not the headlines. Fewer graduate scheme postings, longer waits. I check the job boards already, just to see, and so far the listings look the same as last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the shoe shop tell you about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That customers still want a person to watch them run on the treadmill and say your left foot is rolling in. A website can't do that. I wouldn't bet a career on the shop, but it's a good reminder that some things are better done by a human standing next to you.

say: I'd say the **hype** outran what the tools deliver.
I'd post a **chart** comparing adoption with real productivity.
think: Economics doesn't depend on one **technology**, so I'm fairly relaxed.
My real worry is **money**: three months of rent and a loan.
do: **Keep** the Saturday shifts at the shoe shop.
**Apply** for the department's research assistant scheme.
**Save** 60 a month so I'm not asking Dad.
feel: **Fine**, slightly bored by the lack of a big story.
A little **anxious** about choosing a degree in a hype cycle.
S0.quote: Customers still want a person to watch them run on the treadmill and say your left foot is rolling in.
fieldNote: Treats the world like a **data problem**: wants evidence in job boards, not headlines.
Calm rests on family backing and a small cushion, not blind optimism.
Jokes about his own spreadsheet habit; humour is how he handles worry.

steps.text: Keep fitting shoes at the sports shop on Saturdays
Use the AI tool to check my stats workings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the first time my degree feels like it's about something real. Writing, checking and planning going to software means firms hire differently. I'd bring it up in the econ society, because someone should measure which jobs actually shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy. Entry-level analyst work is reading, summarising, building tables, which is the stuff the tools do already. The people who'd be hired to do it might be me in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the tools now, properly, not just checking maths. I'd learn Python in the second semester and take a data module. And I'd keep an eye on unions and policy, because I'd like to be on the side that shapes how it's shared out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. A bit excited, because it's the biggest thing in my subject in my lifetime. And a bit of a drop in the stomach when I think about a grad scheme with half the places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like to shape how it's shared out. Who gains and who loses in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owners of the software gain, and juniors in white collar jobs lose first. I lean left on this, so I'd want a tax on the gains and public money for retraining. But I know my views don't pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Lucia, who's 14?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To pick things she's curious about, not what sounds safe. I'd tell my sister I don't know what jobs will be there, and anybody who says they do is selling something. And I'd tell her to learn to check the machine's answers instead of trusting it.

say: I'd say it's the first time my degree feels **really relevant**.
I'd ask the econ society to **measure** which jobs actually shrink.
think: Entry-level **analyst work** is the reading and tables the tools already do.
The people squeezed out of those jobs could be **me** in three years.
do: **Learn** Python next semester and take a data module.
**Use** the tools daily to learn their limits.
**Join** the econ society and a policy reading group.
feel: **Excited**, because it's the biggest thing in my subject.
A **drop in the stomach** at grad schemes with half the places.
S1.quote: I'd tell my sister I don't know what jobs will be there, and anybody who says they do is selling something.
fieldNote: Frames the threat as a **measurement** question, which gives him distance.
Moves from calm to anxious because his chosen entry jobs are exactly the exposed ones.
Honest that his progressive views won't pay his rent.

steps.text: Take a Python and data module next semester
Use the AI tool daily and note where it fails
Join the economics society's policy reading group
Ask my tutor which graduate jobs are still hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a policy emergency and nobody's ready. Two years is nothing for governments. I'd be tweeting numbers at my MP and probably getting ratioed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my degree might be worth far less than I'm paying for it. Whatever I'm doing in my seminars, an AI would do it cheaper by the time I'm in third year. And Dad's warehouse job is hands-on, but the planning software over his head would go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in uni because the alternative is nothing, but I'd treat it as buying time. I'd ask the careers service for anything hands-on or regulated, like financial supervision or a trade. And I'd keep the shoe shop weekend job and save everything I can, because cash is the one thing that still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly rattled. It's like being told the exam's moved to tomorrow and the syllabus changed. I'd be joking about it by Thursday, but that's me covering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cash is the one thing that still works. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep it in a boring account, no clever bets. I'd rather have six months of rent than anything fancy. If the world flips there'll be a window where people with money can wait it out, and I'd like to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your parents, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. Mum's school assistant job is probably safe for a while, since kids need adults in the room, but Dad's firm will want to cut the planning team. If he's out of work, the 300 they send me each month stops, and then I'm a student with no safety net.

say: I'd say this is a **policy emergency** and governments aren't ready.
I'd **email** my MP with numbers, even if ignored.
think: My **degree** may be worth much less by third year.
If my dad's **planning team** is cut, the family's help stops.
do: **Stay** at uni, but treat it as buying time.
**Ask** careers for hands-on or regulated work like supervision.
**Save** every spare pound in a boring account.
feel: **Rattled**, like the exam moved to tomorrow.
**Covering** with jokes, though the worry is real.
S2.quote: If the world flips there'll be a window where people with money can wait it out, and I'd like to be one of them.
fieldNote: Humour **masks** real alarm; he says so himself.
The family safety net is the vulnerability: his dad's firm funds his 300 a month.
Reaches for cash and boring choices rather than bold bets.

steps.text: Put every spare pound into a six-month rent fund
Ask the careers service about regulated or hands-on jobs
Email my MP with job-market figures
Look at a trade or financial supervision course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible if we start now. I'd push for the uni to teach people how to work alongside the tools, not pretend they don't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years lands me one year out of graduation. That's the worst timing: I'd be a new graduate in an economy that's just learned it doesn't need new graduates. But it's also enough time to become someone who's useful before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a placement year at a regulator or a central bank, apply to the research assistant scheme, and get good at the tools early. I'd also keep 100 a month back as a buffer. If it gets close, I'd consider doing a master's in public policy to wait out the worst of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. I like having a deadline, even a scary one. It's less nice when I picture my mates who didn't plan, but I can't carry them all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A master's means more debt. How would you weigh that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. If the first jobs are gone, a master's is a way to stay in the system and be near the people making the rules. If the jobs are fine, it's wasted money. So I'd wait until 2030 and look at the job boards before committing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shoe shop be to you by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reminder that I can earn a living standing next to people. If everything goes badly I could manage a store, which is not a failure, it's a wage. I'd rather have that as a floor than be too proud for it.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if we start now.
I'd push the uni to teach **working with the tools**.
think: Five years puts me **one year** out of graduation, the worst timing.
It's also enough time to become **useful** before it hits.
do: **Aim** for a placement year at a regulator or central bank.
**Get good** at the AI tools early.
**Decide** on a policy master's only after checking the job boards in 2030.
feel: **Focused**, because I like a deadline even a scary one.
A little **guilty** about friends who haven't planned.
S3.quote: If everything goes badly I could manage a store, which is not a failure, it's a wage.
fieldNote: Plans in **stages** and builds a fallback he isn't ashamed of.
Timing lands at graduation, which he names as the worst case.
Steady adaptability shows: he commits only after checking evidence.

steps.text: Apply for a placement year at a regulator or central bank
Practise with the AI tools until I know their limits
Hold 100 a month back as a buffer
Check the 2030 job boards before choosing a master's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is what a government needs to rewrite how education and tax work, so we should get on with it. I'd also say it's cheap to prepare and expensive to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. I'd be 28 when it arrives and could have a full career start, savings and maybe a deposit. The risk is that I assume I've got time and drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a proper first job in policy or analysis, and keep learning the tools every year. I'd save as much as I can early, because money invested at 19 is worth a lot at 28. And I'd stay active in politics, because the rules matter more than the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's the same feeling as a long project with a clear deadline: you can pace it. The only bit that nags is that a decade gives people time to look away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might drift. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A checklist, honestly. Every September I'd write down the three things I'd need to be ready for 2036 and tick them off. It sounds silly, but I made a spreadsheet for the house bills and it's worked for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And money over ten years, what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything gets easier. I can pay down the loan, put aside 150 a month, and by 2036 have a cushion that means I could retrain without panicking. In the 2028 picture I'm scrambling. Here I can be generous with my sister, even pay for her course.

say: I'd say it's **cheap to prepare** and expensive to ignore.
I'd push for **education and tax rules** to be rewritten now.
think: I'd feel **pretty good**: a full career start and a cushion by 28.
The risk is **drifting** because ten years feels like plenty.
do: **Finish** the degree and get a first job in policy or analysis.
**Save** 150 a month so a retraining year is affordable.
**Write** a September checklist of three things for 2036.
feel: **Calm**, like pacing a long project with a deadline.
Mild **nag** that a decade gives people time to look away.
S4.quote: I can pay down the loan, put aside 150 a month, and by 2036 have a cushion that means I could retrain without panicking.
fieldNote: Time converts directly into a **savings plan** with numbers.
Self-aware about drift, uses a simple checklist as a guard.
Family-minded: wants to help his sister Lucia, not only himself.

steps.text: Finish the degree and aim for a policy graduate job
Save 150 a month towards a retraining cushion
Learn a new AI tool every September
Plan to help pay for my sister's course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd be in second year, my dad's job could go, and I'd have no time to build a cushion. What would help is a government that already has a plan for retraining and a basic income floor, and universities that tell students the truth about graduate jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume economics students will be fine, but we're probably the most exposed. I'd like someone to say that out loud, so we're not just told to learn to code.

headlineQuote: People assume economics students will be fine, but we're probably the most exposed.
portrait: Ben is an **18-year-old** economics student, wry and numbers-minded, who made a bills spreadsheet for his flat.
He uses AI **now and then** and plans to learn it properly, because he trusts evidence over hype.
His politics lean **left**: taxes on gains, retraining and a floor for those squeezed out.
The weak point is **family money**: his dad's warehouse planning job funds 300 a month.
He swings from calm in the quiet and ten-year worlds to alarm at 2028, using savings and jokes to cope.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his dad's job could go and he'd have no time to save.
whatWouldHelp: A government **retraining plan** and a basic income floor already in place.
Universities that are **honest** about which graduate jobs are shrinking.
